note: An analytical organisation of the evidence. It is not the architecture of any commercial model.

stages.label: Decision contract
stages.question: What exactly is being asked, and what may the answer be?
stages.covers: State, typed question, option names, rubrics, levels, cardinality, abstain options.
stages.evidence: Type validity; name and order invariance; closed-set failure when the right option is missing.

stages.label: Inference & readout
stages.question: How is a distribution over the declared options produced?
stages.covers: Hosted service, encoder heads, frozen or fine-tuned decoder readouts, diffusion reads, generative adapters.
stages.evidence: Same-backbone ablations; readout geometry; what is and is not disclosed.

stages.label: Probability & calibration
stages.question: What does a returned probability or confidence mean, and for which population?
stages.covers: Native vs verbalised probabilities, confidence statistics, ECE/Brier/NLL, recalibration, quantisation.
stages.evidence: Per-task reliability, high-confidence errors, recalibration on held-out labels.

stages.label: Selective control
stages.question: When should software act, ask, escalate or abstain?
stages.covers: Thresholds, risk–coverage, cascades to stronger models, human review budgets.
stages.evidence: Coverage at fixed risk; escalation rate; thresholds chosen on a separate selection set.

stages.label: Downstream use
stages.question: Does the whole workflow get better, cheaper or faster?
stages.covers: End-task success, end-to-end latency, cost per correct completion, derived quantities.
stages.evidence: System-level baselines; module attribution; matched measurement scope.

method_families.label: Hosted System One service
method_families.principle: A closed, hosted model returns a distribution over declared options for each typed question about a shared text state.
method_families.disclosed: Interface, primitives, pricing, limits, versioning and known failure modes are documented; architecture, training data and the exact confidence statistic are not.
method_families.boundary: Black-box evaluation only; the served model can change behind aliases; text-only input.

method_families.label: Encoder decision heads
method_families.principle: A bidirectional encoder, or an encoder–decoder, reads state, question and options; a trained head scores each option and a softmax is taken over the legal set.
method_families.disclosed: Weights and inference code for most members; several release training code; the readout geometry (marker token, span mean, blind per-option scoring) changes name and order sensitivity.
method_families.boundary: Short context windows; option labels can dominate written definitions; adjacent to GLiClass, SetFit and NLI zero-shot classifiers.

method_families.label: Frozen decoder option readout
method_families.principle: An unmodified causal LM is prompted once and the next-token logits of short option identifiers are renormalised over the declared options, optionally debiased over label priors and option rotations.
method_families.disclosed: Fully open and training-free; a frozen 4B model read this way matches community fine-tunes on public JevBench items — the natural baseline for any trained decision model.
method_families.boundary: Raw logits are order- and label-sensitive; one prefill cannot reason; rotation averaging multiplies cost by the number of rotations.

method_families.label: Fine-tuned decoder decision models
method_families.principle: A decoder is adapted (LoRA or full fine-tuning) so that a designated position or pointer head yields calibrated option probabilities in one pass.
method_families.disclosed: Many release weights, training code and evaluation data; lineages exist (this-that-model is adapted from decider-2b; SecJev builds on Kev); task-specialised variants beat general ones on their own tasks.
method_families.boundary: Gains may come from task coverage in training; benchmarks are often built by the same teams; derived checkpoints are not independent methods.

method_families.label: Diffusion structured readout
method_families.principle: A discrete diffusion LM is seeded with the answer template; after one denoising step, the distribution at each answer slot is read directly.
method_families.disclosed: Open servers with a Jev-compatible wire API; depends on request extensions proposed in an unmerged vLLM PR.
method_families.boundary: A different mechanism from last-token decoder readout; custom entropy-based confidence.

method_families.label: Generative & constrained adapters
method_families.principle: A general LLM is asked (often under JSON-schema constraints) to emit a decision and probabilities, which are validated and returned in Jev-shaped responses.
method_families.disclosed: Wire compatibility for controlled comparisons; probabilities are generated or verbalised, not read from logits.
method_families.boundary: Interface compatibility is not mechanism equivalence; retries, parsing and self-reported probabilities remain.

openness_statuses.restricted: Exists but access is limited by licence or data agreement.
openness_statuses.claimed_not_located: The paper says it is released, but it was not located.
openness_statuses.not_located: Not located (not evidence that it does not exist).
openness_statuses.project_page_only: Only a project page or result files are public.
openness_statuses.not_applicable: Does not apply (e.g. weights of a hosted commercial service).
openness_statuses.not_attempted: This review did not attempt independent reproduction.
openness_statuses.no: Cannot be recomputed from the located materials.

findings.title: A type-valid answer can still be the wrong answer.
findings.body: Typed interfaces remove parse and schema failures by construction. They do not ensure that the model reads the options the way the author meant: short labels can outweigh written definitions, rebinding names to rubrics can reverse a ranking, a middle option can absorb errors, and when the right answer is missing the model usually picks a wrong option instead of the exit. Order effects can change many individual answers while aggregate accuracy stays flat. The type-error rate stays at zero throughout.

findings.title: A native probability makes calibration measurable, not guaranteed.
findings.body: Every call returns a distribution, so reliability can be audited on each run. Measured calibration varies by task, construct and language; probabilities can rank well yet sit badly against a fixed threshold; temperatures fitted on a few options transfer poorly to many; and confidence stays high where the model lacks the knowledge. Thresholds and recalibration fitted on separate data help, but only for the workload they were fitted on.

findings.title: The most consistent use is a bounded first pass with confidence-gated escalation.
findings.body: Across judging, annotation, moderation, intrusion detection, infrastructure triage and agents, the typed model is usually cheaper and faster but not the most accurate component. Gains appear when uncertain cases go to a stronger model or a person and thresholds are frozen on separate data; the strongest designs fix them in advance and test on new workloads. Savings shrink once pre-screen costs, held-out misses and cheap trained classifiers are counted, so those belong in the comparison.

findings.title: Speed and cost claims decompose into different mechanisms and scopes.
findings.body: Single-request latency, per-question amortized time, batch throughput, end-to-end task time, deadline attainment under load, simulated timing and API bills are different quantities. Prefix sharing, batching, caching and pruning can explain as much as the readout does; billing every option as input can erase the price advantage against batch-priced LLMs; and a faster step can make a slower agent. None of the figures can be pooled into a single leaderboard.

findings.title: Interface compatibility is not mechanism equivalence.
findings.body: Open projects reproduce the request and response shape with encoders, encoder–decoders, frozen or fine-tuned decoders, diffusion reads and task-specialised models, and a frozen instruction-tuned LLM read through option identifiers can match community Jev-style models built on the same backbone. Their probabilities come from different mechanisms, they differ in what is released and in how reproducible they are, and none establishes the architecture of the commercial model. Rankings between hosted and open models change from task to task.

findings.title: System-level gains need module-level attribution and the right reference.
findings.body: Memory systems, query engines, search agents, orchestration pipelines and scientific workflows improve for many reasons at once. Attribution requires ablations, matched baselines and references that measure what the workflow reuses. When code owns pruning, lookahead or simulation, the typed model can serve as a strong evaluator; when one call must both simulate and evaluate, or step errors compound over a long trajectory, the system gets worse even as each step gets faster.

findings.title: The evidence base is young, clustered and unreplicated.
findings.body: The core preprints appeared within weeks of the launch, mostly as a single version, and several were substantially revised soon after. Several author groups contribute more than one study, some benchmarks are built by teams that also rank their own models, many community results are self-reported, and one study’s audit of its own pipeline corrected its headline deployment numbers. Hosted answers drift from day to day. None of the core results has been independently reproduced.

findings.title: A calibrated probability is not a coherent belief.
findings.body: Probabilities from the same model can break basic rules across related questions (a statement and its negation, single labels and their union), change the decision when the same question is asked through another interface, and pile mass on the most likely option far beyond its true chance. Average calibration certifies none of this. Check coherence across complementary questions and interfaces before treating outputs as beliefs, and prefer uses that only need the ranking.

findings.title: Typed decisions read what the input states; they do not reliably compute what it implies.
findings.body: Studies of arithmetic menus, exact numbers, graph structure, packet and sensor values, games and planning meet the same boundary: answers are strong when the needed fact is written in the state and weak when it must be counted, calculated or simulated. The vendor’s own guidance is to count, convert and compare in code. Letting code compute or simulate and asking the model to evaluate the result works better. Calculation-heavy benchmark items can still look easy when they may have been seen in training.

findings.title: A typed output does not make a decision safe from its inputs.
findings.body: Because the answer depends on the state, text placed in the state can move it. Injected text rarely reached an attacker’s target in one study, while in another both context-ignoring injections and injections that supply false facts redirected nearly every decision; natural context and appended opinions flip confident answers; poisoned open checkpoints carry backdoors with clean accuracy intact; and confidence gates can themselves be attacked to drain capacity. Constrained outputs limit what an attacker can make the model say, not what it decides.

failure_modes.title: Option names outweigh the rubric
failure_modes.desc: Rebinding which rubric sits behind “no/yes” moves answers far more than the same swap behind neutral names, and a yes/no swap flipped half of the hosted model’s answers in another study; a 0% type-error rate hides both.
failure_modes.mitigation: Neutral identifiers with meaning carried in the rubric; name-invariance checks next to type-error rates.

failure_modes.title: Labels outweigh definitions
failure_modes.desc: In open typed-decision models the answer followed the short option label rather than its written definition, and supplying a dataset’s definition moved up to 28% of predictions without reliably improving them.
failure_modes.mitigation: Test with neutral labels and with labels that contradict their definitions; render options so the definition, not the label, carries the rule.

failure_modes.title: Order flips hide in aggregates
failure_modes.desc: One audit found no order flips on hosted Jev, yet four cyclic rotations changed 37% of answers item by item in another study; open readouts flipped on a third of 20-option items, and the vendor now lists option order among Jev’s known weaknesses.
failure_modes.mitigation: Report per-item flip rates under rotation next to aggregate accuracy; average over rotations or isolate candidates.

failure_modes.title: The primitive changes the answer
failure_modes.desc: A Noul and a two-option Choice over the same question can disagree, the choice of primitive can reverse a comparison with an LLM baseline, and asking the same probability through two interfaces changed the act/defer decision on a third of pairs.
failure_modes.mitigation: Fix the primitive in a protocol; test both when a result depends on it.

failure_modes.title: Missing answers go unnoticed
failure_modes.desc: When the right answer is absent the model usually picks a wrong option rather than the exit: 7% correct rejection of arithmetic menus with an explicit “None”, 24.8% detection of a removed reference label, few “I don’t know” choices on unanswerable questions.
failure_modes.mitigation: Keep an explicit exit, verify candidates with separate yes/no questions, and fit a rejection threshold on held-out answer-absent cases.

failure_modes.title: Middle options absorb errors
failure_modes.desc: On ANLI the Neutral option took 51% of errors at every candidate position, and across 36 ordinal datasets decisions used only about two-thirds to three-quarters of the gold scale.
failure_modes.mitigation: Check how much of the label scale predictions use; compare ordinal and nominal framings of the same items.

failure_modes.title: Injected state redirects decisions
failure_modes.desc: Text placed in the state moved decisions — from rarely reaching an attacker’s target with instruction-style injections to near-certain redirection when the injection supplies false facts; natural context flipped 61% of correct decisions in another study.
failure_modes.mitigation: Separate trusted from untrusted state, verify facts in code, and red-team with false-state injections, not only instructions.

failure_modes.title: Vendor-listed jagged edges
failure_modes.desc: The vendor lists literal reading, math and numbers, date comparison, indirection, large irrelevant state, adversarial content, contradictory criteria, option order and generation as known weak spots of jev-1.13.
failure_modes.mitigation: Keep arithmetic and date logic in code; filter state; split indirect questions; re-check answers under reordered options.

failure_modes.title: Consistent is not correct
failure_modes.desc: A model can return the same wrong label under every request condition and repeat; agreement across repeats then hides a stable error.
failure_modes.mitigation: Score every repeat against gold labels and report stable errors separately from changing ones.

failure_modes.title: Same request, different answer
failure_modes.desc: Repeated identical requests to the hosted model do not always return the same answer — a re-run changed the Score value on 38.5% of Score questions in one study and 0.5% of decisions a day later in another — while an open checkpoint reproduced bit-for-bit.
failure_modes.mitigation: Measure a test–retest floor and report effects relative to it.

failure_modes.title: Cacheable scoring loses the rules
failure_modes.desc: Encoding candidates independently so they can be cached cut rule-sensitive recall from 1.00 to 0.24; isolating candidates removes order effects only if the rules stay in view.
failure_modes.mitigation: Keep the state and rules in every candidate’s view; re-measure rule sensitivity after any caching change.

failure_modes.title: Poisoned open checkpoints
failure_modes.desc: Poisoning 5% of an open model’s training records implanted backdoors that redirected most targeted inputs while clean accuracy stayed above 90%.
failure_modes.mitigation: Pin checkpoints by hash and source, and prefer releases whose training data and recipe are documented.

failure_modes.title: Confident on the wrong construct
failure_modes.desc: Calibration varies by task: on one construct the model was confident while near chance, and audits disagree across datasets.
failure_modes.mitigation: Audit reliability per task and construct, not with one global ECE.

failure_modes.title: Probabilities that do not add up
failure_modes.desc: P(X) and P(not X) missed 1 by 0.064 on average, three single-label probabilities summed to 1.14, and the most likely option received 89% of the mass where its true chance was 36%.
failure_modes.mitigation: Ask complementary questions and check sums; use rankings rather than raw magnitudes where coherence was not tested.

failure_modes.title: Confident beyond what it knows
failure_modes.desc: With no answer-relevant information the model still put up to 0.80 on a salient option, and on news past its knowledge boundary confidence exceeded accuracy by 0.21–0.33 even after recalibration on earlier months.
failure_modes.mitigation: Ask targeted yes/no questions about whether the evidence suffices; do not read low confidence as missing knowledge.

failure_modes.title: Unknowable rules and distribution shift
failure_modes.desc: On labels not recoverable from the text, probabilities stayed concentrated; a large post-hoc temperature was needed to make them honest.
failure_modes.mitigation: Hold out domains and rule changes; recalibrate on target-domain labels.

failure_modes.title: Language shift costs accuracy
failure_modes.desc: A Spanish state with English instructions lost accuracy on every tested dataset, calibration worsened on the hardest tasks, and persona shifts reproduced a smaller share of human differences in Arabic than in English.
failure_modes.mitigation: Evaluate in the deployment language; pin the model version.

failure_modes.title: Two-decimal probabilities
failure_modes.desc: Probabilities are returned on a 0.01 grid, which puts a floor under calibration error for rare events and can place exactly zero on a correct answer.
failure_modes.mitigation: Treat rare-event probabilities with care; smooth before log-loss.

failure_modes.title: Thresholds that do not travel
failure_modes.desc: A threshold set for 5% in-scope risk still admitted 31% of out-of-scope requests, binary probabilities ranked well but sat badly against 0.5, and in-sample thresholds aimed at 5% misses gave up to 17% on held-out data.
failure_modes.mitigation: Fit thresholds on held-out data from the deployment distribution, per option count, and re-check after any version change.

failure_modes.title: Asked to compute, it estimates
failure_modes.desc: Exact numbers, counts, graph degrees, packet statistics and opponents’ moves must be computed or simulated, and typed answers land near rather than on them: 44% exact on repeating division (97% within one), 68% on vertex degree, 28% on packet-based traffic classes.
failure_modes.mitigation: Compute in code and ask the model to judge the result; supply simulations or lookahead explicitly.

failure_modes.title: Fast steps, slower agent
failure_modes.desc: Replacing an agent’s action selection with a typed model cut median episode time but lowered success from 77.6% to 66.1% and lengthened the slowest runs as step errors compounded.
failure_modes.mitigation: Evaluate at the episode level, including tail latency and success, not per step.

failure_modes.title: Validity effects masquerade as quality
failure_modes.desc: When comparing with generative baselines, parse failures and repairs change accuracy independently of reasoning; typed outputs remove the failure but not the confound in comparisons.
failure_modes.mitigation: Count invalid outputs as errors and report parse rates separately.

failure_modes.title: Right label, wrong quantity
failure_modes.desc: A wrong intermediate selection can change a derived count while leaving the final label correct.
failure_modes.mitigation: Score intermediate relations and derived quantities, not only final labels.

application_cards.decides: Gates, approvals and rule applications inside business workflows: route, accept, reject or escalate.
application_cards.caution: Trained classifiers win when labels exist; missing answers and many-option thresholds are weak spots.

application_cards.decides: Which of two responses is better, whether an answer is supported, how a rubric criterion is met.
application_cards.caution: Falls behind where the verdict must be derived (math, code, logic); judges can share its confident errors.

application_cards.decides: Labels for social-science text, political replications and crash narratives, with a probability per label.
application_cards.caution: Per-construct failures; no cost advantage against batch-priced LLMs; one author group contributes several studies.

application_cards.decides: Intrusion, injection, trace-safety and vulnerability triage decisions — and the security of the decision layer itself.
application_cards.caution: A strong detector whose own decisions can be redirected through the state.

application_cards.decides: Hate-speech moderation and failure detection against written policies.
application_cards.caution: Supplied definitions move many answers without reliably improving them.

application_cards.decides: Which tool, action or branch an agent takes next, escalating to a stronger model when unsure.
application_cards.caution: Faster steps can make a slower, less successful agent; let code supply lookahead and simulation.

application_cards.decides: Relevance, evidence sufficiency and next search actions; reranking retrieved candidates.
application_cards.caution: Specialised open models beat Jev on some search decisions; hosted latency includes network overhead.

application_cards.decides: How memories are typed, selected and retrieved, and when retrieval stops.
application_cards.caution: System-level gains measured against different baselines.

application_cards.decides: Intent fields, A1 policies, traffic classes and alarm causes in networks and water infrastructure.
application_cards.caution: Meets second-scale control deadlines, not 100 ms ones; raw numeric features defeat it; one author group contributes three studies.

application_cards.decides: Medical questions, surveillance from narratives, imaging decisions and speech rescoring.
application_cards.caution: Parity on abstracts but large gaps on diagnostic cases; none of this is clinical validation.

application_cards.decides: Semantic filters, joins and rankings inside SQL; structural questions about graphs.
application_cards.caution: Pruning carries much of the gain; graph structure has to be computed, not read.

application_cards.decides: Image questions with an independent visual model, and decisions from video, pixel or sensor features rendered as text.
application_cards.caution: Hosted Jev is text-only; numeric features rendered as text lose to trained models.

application_cards.decides: Moves in games, navigation steps and robot skills chosen from short candidate lists.
application_cards.caution: Plays as if the opponent were random unless the opponent’s move is stated.

application_cards.decides: The distribution of a described respondent’s survey answers, once per unique state.
application_cards.caution: Fails intervention-sensitivity gates without flagship anchors; two human-referenced tests.

application_cards.decides: Entailment, contradiction or no mention for each hypothesis about one contract.
application_cards.caution: Cheapest and fastest, but below every hosted LLM on accuracy; small stability panel.

application_cards.decides: Which scientific relation governs a calculation that code then performs.
application_cards.caution: Twenty Choices in ten cases; not discriminative across strong models.
